section.title: AI & Mathematics
section.label: Section One
section.description: The vocabulary of machine learning, statistics, optimisation and the linear algebra underneath all of it. Every entry is defined in terms a reader can substitute back into a sentence, then anchored to the paper or theorem it came from.

definitions.text: an iterative procedure that reduces a differentiable objective by repeatedly stepping in the direction opposite to its slope at the current point.
definitions.example: Training halted once gradient descent stopped lowering the validation objective.

definitions.text: the family of training algorithms that update model parameters from the slope of a loss surface, including the stochastic and mini-batch variants used in practice.
definitions.example: Nearly every deep network in production was fitted by some form of gradient descent.

formula.note: eta is the step size, or learning rate; grad J is the slope of the objective at the current parameters.

entries.etymology: From gradient, Latin gradiens 'stepping', plus descent, Old French descente 'a going down'. Named for the geometric picture of walking downhill on a surface.

citations.label: Cauchy, A. (1847). Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d'équations simultanées.
citations.source: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, 25, 536–538.

citations.label: Robbins, H. & Monro, S. (1951). A Stochastic Approximation Method.

definitions.text: an application of the chain rule that computes the sensitivity of a loss to every parameter in a layered network by passing partial derivatives from the output back toward the input.
definitions.example: One backpropagation pass yields every parameter's derivative in roughly the cost of one forward pass.

formula.plain: dL/dW(l) = delta(l) * a(l-1)^T,  delta(l) = W(l+1)^T * delta(l+1) .* sigma'(z(l))
formula.note: delta is the error signal at a layer; the circled dot is elementwise multiplication.

entries.etymology: A 1980s contraction of 'backward propagation of errors'. Popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986, though the underlying reverse-mode differentiation was described by Linnainmaa in 1970.

citations.label: Rumelhart, D., Hinton, G. & Williams, R. (1986). Learning representations by back-propagating errors.
Linnainmaa, S. (1970). The representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors.

definitions.text: the failure mode in which a model absorbs noise particular to its training sample and therefore predicts unseen data worse than a simpler model would.
definitions.example: Validation error rose while training error kept falling — textbook overfitting.

formula.note: Overfitting is the regime where the variance term dominates the decomposition.

entries.etymology: From over- 'excessively' plus fit, in the statistical sense of fitting a curve to points; in use in the regression literature from the mid-twentieth century.

citations.label: Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R. & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, ch. 7.

definitions.text: a non-zero vector whose direction is unchanged by a given linear map, so the map merely rescales it by a constant factor.
definitions.example: The covariance matrix's leading eigenvector points along the axis of greatest spread in the data.

formula.note: lambda is the eigenvalue: the factor by which the map stretches that direction.

entries.etymology: A partial calque of German Eigenvektor, from eigen 'own, characteristic'. Hilbert used Eigenwert in 1904; the hybrid German-English form settled into English mathematics in the 1920s–30s.

citations.label: Strang, G. (2016). Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th ed., ch. 6.

definitions.text: a layer that produces each output as a weighted blend of all available inputs, where the weights are computed from the similarity between a query and a set of keys.
definitions.example: The attention mechanism let the decoder consult any source token instead of a single fixed summary vector.

formula.note: Division by sqrt(d_k) keeps the dot products in a range where softmax gradients do not vanish.

entries.etymology: Borrowed from cognitive psychology, where attention names the selective allocation of processing. Introduced to neural machine translation by Bahdanau et al. in 2014.

citations.label: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K. & Bengio, Y. (2015). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate.
Vaswani, A. et al. (2017). Attention Is All You Need.

definitions.text: the identity that converts the likelihood of evidence given a hypothesis into the probability of the hypothesis given that evidence, by weighting it with the hypothesis's prior probability.
definitions.example: Applying Bayes' theorem to a positive test result requires the disease's base rate, not just the test's accuracy.

formula.note: P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(A|B) the posterior.

entries.etymology: An eponym (Rule 519) after Thomas Bayes (c. 1701–1761), the English Presbyterian minister whose essay on the problem was published posthumously by Richard Price in 1763.

citations.label: Bayes, T. & Price, R. (1763). An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances.
citations.source: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 53, 370–418.

definitions.text: a measure of the difference between predicted and actual values, quantifying the error of a model's output.
definitions.example: We must select an appropriate loss function, such as Mean Squared Error, to guide the model's training process.

formula.note: This example shows the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function.

entries.etymology: From loss, Old English los 'destruction, ruin', plus function, Latin functio 'performance'. The technical sense — a function assigning a penalty to a decision — comes from Abraham Wald's statistical decision theory of the 1940s, which borrowed the economic sense of loss.

citations.label: Goodfellow et al. (2016). Deep Learning, ch. 6.

definitions.text: a hyperparameter that controls the step size taken at each iteration of an optimization algorithm.
definitions.example: If the learning rate is too high, the optimization process may overshoot the minimum loss.

formula.latex:
w_{t+1} = w_t -  rac{	ext{learning rate}}{	ext{gradient}} 
abla L(w_t)
formula.plain: w_t+1 = w_t - (learning rate / gradient) * grad L(w_t)
formula.note: The learning rate determines the magnitude of the step taken in the direction opposite to the gradient.

entries.etymology: From learning, Old English leornian 'to acquire knowledge', plus rate, Medieval Latin rata (pars) 'a fixed amount'. Compounded in the cybernetics literature of the late 1950s, where it named the constant scaling the correction applied at each training step.

citations.label: Goodfellow et al. (2016). Deep Learning, ch. 8.

definitions.text: a technique used to prevent overfitting by adding a penalty term to the loss function, which discourages overly complex models.
definitions.example: We applied L2 regularization to the model to prevent overfitting on the training data.

formula.note: The penalty term controls the complexity of the model weights (w).

entries.etymology: From Latin regula 'rule', via regularis 'according to rule'. The mathematical sense — constraining an ill-posed problem until it becomes well-posed — is due to Andrey Tikhonov, whose work gives the method its other name, Tikhonov regularization.

citations.label: Tikhonov, A. (1963). Regularization in ill-posed problems.

definitions.text: an architecture that slides a small set of learned filters across grid-structured input, so the same local pattern is recognised wherever it appears and far fewer weights are needed than a fully connected design.
definitions.example: A convolutional neural network reached human-level accuracy on the digit set with a fraction of the parameters.

formula.note: The discrete convolution each filter applies at every position.

entries.etymology: From convolution, Latin convolvere 'to roll together', naming the integral operation the layers perform, plus neural network. The architecture descends from Fukushima's neocognitron of 1980 and was given its modern trainable form by LeCun and colleagues in 1989.

citations.label: LeCun, Y. et al. (1989). Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition.
Fukushima, K. (1980). Neocognitron: A self-organizing neural network model for a mechanism of pattern recognition.

definitions.text: a function that takes a vector of real numbers and maps it to a probability distribution, ensuring that all elements are positive and sum to one.
definitions.example: We applied the Softmax function to the final layer's logits to get class probabilities.

formula.note: z is the vector of raw scores (logits), and K is the number of classes.

entries.etymology: A compound of soft and max, naming a smooth relaxation of the maximum: where max returns a single winner, this returns a graded distribution over all candidates. Named by John Bridle in 1990, who introduced it as a differentiable stand-in for winner-take-all selection.

citations.label: Goodfellow et al. (2016). Deep Learning, ch. 7.

definitions.text: a technique used to estimate the performance of a model on unseen data by partitioning the dataset into multiple subsets.
definitions.example: We used k-fold Cross-Validation to ensure our model's performance was robust across different data splits.

entries.etymology: From cross- 'crosswise, reciprocally' plus validation, Latin validus 'strong'. The prefix names the reciprocal arrangement in which each subset serves in turn as the held-out set. Resampling of this kind appears in the 1930s; the method was formalised and named by Stone and by Geisser, independently, in 1974.

citations.label: Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., ch. 5.

definitions.text: a measure of the uncertainty or randomness inherent in a random variable or source of data.
definitions.example: The high entropy of the source indicated that the data was highly unpredictable.

formula.note: The base-2 logarithm yields the unit of bits.

entries.etymology: From Greek entropein, meaning 'to transform' or 'to change', adopted into thermodynamics by Rudolf Clausius.

citations.label: Cover, T. M., & Thomas, J. A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed., ch. 2.

definitions.text: a sequence of random variables where the probability of transitioning to the next state depends only on the current state, and not on the sequence of states that preceded it.
definitions.example: We modeled the weather transitions using a Markov Chain to predict the next day's conditions.

formula.note: This property is known as the Markov property.

entries.etymology: Named after the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov, who introduced the concept in the early 20th century.

citations.label: Nagaraja, K. (2018). Introduction to Stochastic Processes, 2nd ed., ch. 3.

definitions.text: a neural network architecture that relies solely on attention mechanisms, allowing it to process sequential data efficiently.
definitions.example: The Transformer model revolutionized sequence-to-sequence tasks by eliminating recurrence.

formula.plain: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
formula.note: The core mechanism involves scaled dot-product attention.

entries.etymology: Coined by the authors of the seminal 2017 paper, drawing inspiration from the concept of transforming data representations.

citations.label: Vaswani et al. (2017). Attention Is All You Need.

definitions.text: a low-dimensional vector representation of high-dimensional data, such as words or images, that captures semantic or structural relationships.
definitions.example: We trained a word2vec model to generate a dense vector embedding for each word in the corpus.

formula.note: W is the weight matrix, x is the input vector, and b is the bias.

entries.etymology: Coined by Tomas Mikolov in 2013, derived from the general concept of mapping complex data into a continuous vector space.

citations.label: Mikolov et al. (2013). Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space.

definitions.text: a training paradigm in which an agent improves its policy purely from rewards collected while acting in an environment, with no labelled examples of correct behaviour to imitate.
definitions.example: Reinforcement learning taught the arm to grasp without anyone demonstrating the motion.

formula.plain: Q(s,a) <- Q(s,a) + alpha [ r + gamma max_a' Q(s',a') - Q(s,a) ]
formula.note: The Q-learning update. gamma discounts future reward; alpha is the step size.

entries.etymology: From reinforcement, the term Pavlov's translators used for a stimulus that strengthens a conditioned response, itself from Latin re- 'again' plus fortis 'strong'. Carried into machine learning from animal-behaviour psychology by Minsky in the 1950s.

citations.label: Sutton, R. & Barto, A. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.
Watkins, C. & Dayan, P. (1992). Q-learning.

definitions.text: the fundamental tension between the complexity of a model and its ability to generalize to unseen data.
definitions.example: Understanding the Bias-Variance Tradeoff is crucial for selecting the appropriate regularization strength.

formula.note: The total expected error is the sum of squared bias, variance, and irreducible error.

entries.etymology: From bias, Old French biais 'a slant', by way of the statistical sense of a systematic offset from the truth, plus variance, Latin variantia 'difference'. The decomposition that names the tradeoff was set out by Stuart Geman, Elie Bienenstock and René Doursat in 1992.

citations.label: Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., ch. 6.

definitions.text: a transformation that rewrites correlated measurements as a smaller set of uncorrelated axes, ordered so the first captures as much of the spread as any single direction can.
definitions.example: Principal component analysis reduced the 200 sensor channels to six axes that retained 94% of the variance.

formula.plain: C = (1/(n-1)) X^T X,   C v_i = lambda_i v_i
formula.note: The axes are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ranked by their eigenvalues.

entries.etymology: From principal, Latin principalis 'first, chief', plus component, Latin componere 'to put together'. Introduced by Karl Pearson in 1901 as a line of closest fit, and named and developed independently by Harold Hotelling in 1933.

citations.label: Pearson, K. (1901). On Lines and Planes of Closest Fit to Systems of Points in Space.
Hotelling, H. (1933). Analysis of a complex of statistical variables into principal components.

definitions.text: a method that picks the parameter values under which the observed data would have been most probable, by maximising the probability the model assigns to that data.
definitions.example: Maximum likelihood estimation gives the sample mean as the estimator for a Gaussian's centre.

formula.plain: theta_hat = argmax_theta sum_i log p(x_i | theta)
formula.note: The log turns a product into a sum without moving the maximum.

entries.etymology: From Latin maximus 'greatest' and aestimare 'to value', with likelihood, Middle English liklihede, in the technical sense Ronald Fisher gave it in 1922 to distinguish it from probability: a function of the parameter given fixed data, not of the data.

citations.label: Fisher, R. A. (1922). On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics.
citations.source: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 222, 309–368.
